title: Merrick People in Early Land Records
summary: The history preserves Indigenous names that appear in early records connected with Merrick/Mericock, Massapequa, Rockaway, Hempstead, and neighboring western Long Island communities. Some people are represented by fuller biography pages because the references gives enough context. Others appear mainly as deed signers, witnesses, or named representatives, so their names are kept here without inventing life stories the records do not support.
content:
Purpose

People with Fuller Merrick-Connected Biographies

  • Tackapousha, a Massapequa leader connected with the 1643 Hempstead deed, the 1657 Hempstead conference, and the 1675 Mercock land challenge.
  • Wyandanch, a Montaukett sachem connected with the 1657 Hempstead conference.
  • Cockenoe, an interpreter and diplomat connected with the 1657 Hempstead conference.
  • Mangwobe, a Rockaway sachem named in connection with the 1657 Hempstead conference.
  • Adam (Achitteronose), a Native diplomat connected with the 1656 Dutch treaty context that included Meracock/Merrick and neighboring western Long Island communities.

Names Preserved from Thin Records

The 1643 Hempstead deed and related references preserve several additional Indigenous names, including Jorrane or Iarane/Aarane, Pamaman, Remos or Remoj, Wamis or Waines, Whanege or Whanage, and Gerasco or Yarafus. The records connect these names collectively with Native representation involving Massapequa, Merrick/Merriack, and Rockaway, but they do not clearly separate each person's community affiliation or provide enough life detail for responsible individual biographies.

Other related western Long Island records preserve names such as Piscamoc, Wattewochkouw, Kachpolhor, Ketachkwawars, Waghtummoore, Wogquatis, Uppahanuum, Rumegie or Pers-roma, Wangwang, Rumassaskromen, Woronmcacking, Sayasstock, Martom, Ramerock Drummer, Manockeamicoke, Sashamosse, Mattacaman, Wow-house, and John Smith. These names remain important, even when the surviving public record is brief.

Why Names Matter

Colonial land records often survive because they served colonial ownership claims. Reading them only as property records can hide Native presence, diplomacy, translation, kinship, and resistance. Preserving these names carefully keeps Merrick Ancestral Land visible as a living Native history landscape rather than only a place-name on a modern map.
why_this_matters: The names of Merrick people in early land records preserve Indigenous presence, diplomacy, and memory while avoiding invented biography from thin evidence. Merrick Ancestral Land includes named Native people as well as places.
